Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{2y}{x}\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper-right quarter of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{2y}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{2\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(3\operatorname{tan}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{3x}{y}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper-left quarter of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-3,0),$ as shown above.
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{3x}{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }3\operatorname{cot}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =-9[\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =-9(0-1) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $2,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(0,-2),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩.

a
16∫π3π/2sin⁡tcos3⁡tdt
b
8∫π3π/2sin⁡tcos3⁡tdt
c
4∫π3π/2(sin⁡t+cos2⁡t)dt
d

Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 2 centered at O. It can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩,π≤t≤3π2.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(2sin⁡t)=2cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=x2y, we obtain f(r(t))=(2cos⁡t)2⋅2sin⁡t=8sin⁡tcos2⁡t.

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $2,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(0,-2),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(9−y2)dy, where C is the path along three-quarters of the ellipse 9x2+y2=9, traversed from the point (0,3) to the point (1,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩.

a
27∫π/22πcos3⁡tdt
b
18∫π/22πcos2⁡tdt
c
18∫π/22πsin3⁡tdt
d
27∫π/22πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
e
9∫π/22πsin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: The indicated path has π/2≤t≤2π. Since y=3sin(t), dy=3cos(t)dt and 9-y²=9cos²(t). Thus the integral becomes 27∫_{π/2}^{2π}cos³(t)dt, which is option a.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066119/assets/69a10b5524670d31cfc9f2982e37d58a5ee9ca39fe49f35b9dace011275a635a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(9-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along three-quarters of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(1,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9-(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =9-9{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =9(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }9{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(9−y2)dy, where C is the path along three-quarters of the ellipse 9x2+y2=9, traversed from the point (0,3) to the point (1,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩.

a
27∫π/22πcos3⁡tdt
b
18∫π/22πcos2⁡tdt
c
18∫π/22πsin3⁡tdt
d
27∫π/22πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
e
9∫π/22πsin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩,π2≤t≤2π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(3sin⁡t)=3cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=9−y2, we obtain f(r(t))=9−(3sin⁡t)2=9−9sin2⁡t=9(1−sin2⁡t)=9cos2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫π/22πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫π/22π9cos2⁡t⋅3cos⁡tdt=27∫π/22πcos3⁡tdt.

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(9-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along three-quarters of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(1,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9-(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =9-9{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =9(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }9{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
